implementation_notes: Rails replaced the transactional-queue structure with callback semantics: Active Record callbacks such as after_save run inside the transaction and are rolled back with it, so publication must hang off after_commit - which fires only once the transaction is durable - while after_rollback discards it; Active Job 7.2+ defers enqueueing automatically through enqueue_after_transaction_commit and drops the job if the transaction rolls back. That is the idiomatic replacement: the queue stays external and non-transactional while the enqueue becomes commit-ordered. The classic form (a queue table written in the same database transaction, i.e. an outbox or a database-backed job table) is still justified when the message must not be lost at all, because the row commits with the business data and a worker publishes it later.
code_sketch:
Order.transaction do
  order = Order.create!(params)
  Outbox.create!(topic: "orders", payload: order.to_json)   # commits with the row
end
# or commit-ordered publication (Rails 7.2 defers the enqueue to after commit):
Order.transaction { Order.create!(params).tap { |o| PublishOrderJob.perform_later(o.id) } }
pitfalls: Enqueueing or publishing from inside the transaction (a plain perform_later before 7.2, an HTTP call, a broker client) lets a worker or the broker see work that a later rollback erases; use after_commit or enqueue_after_transaction_commit.
after_commit runs after the commit but nothing retries it: a crash in between loses the publication, so use an outbox row when the message must survive.
With multiple databases (connected_to / role switching) the callback fires per connection commit, and a transaction that raises ActiveRecord::Rollback swallows the error instead of propagating it.
